title: Search Autocomplete (Type-Ahead)
problem: Design a top-k search autocomplete system that returns the 5 most popular queries for a typed prefix within 100ms.
summary: A read-dominated system for 10M DAU that returns top-5 completions for each keystroke under 100ms. The dominant design choice is a trie with top-k precomputed at every node (serving is O(1) after the prefix walk), populated by an offline batch pipeline (analytics logs → aggregator → worker builds trie → Trie Cache + Trie DB) that rebuilds weekly. Online path: Client → LB → API → Trie Cache (with fallback to Trie DB). The main tradeoff is freshness vs serving simplicity: an in-memory trie is blazing fast to read but rebuild cadence (weekly in the book's base design) means trending queries lag until the next cycle — the book's 'how to support real-time' follow-up outlines stream processing as the fix. A filter layer in front of the cache removes hateful/violent/NSFW suggestions; a shard-map manager handles prefix-shard imbalance.

functional: Return the top 5 autocomplete suggestions for any typed prefix
Support per-keystroke requests with sub-100ms p99 latency
Rank suggestions by historical query frequency over a trailing window
Filter hateful, violent, and NSFW phrases out of the returned list
Rebuild the suggestion index from raw query logs on a daily or weekly cadence
Support prefix-only matching in ASCII English in the base design
nonFunctional: p99 response time under 100ms at the 48K peak QPS target
Availability of at least 99.9% on the read path
Bounded memory per node: trie cache fits in RAM on each replica
Freshness SLA: new trending queries visible within one rebuild cycle

assumptions: 10 searches/user/day, ~20 characters avg per query → 20 requests per query (one per keystroke)
Query string ≈ 20 bytes (4 words × 5 chars, ASCII)
~20% of daily queries are new → ~0.4 GB/day of new data (book's calc)
Matching is prefix-only (not mid-string), English lowercase only in base design
Response-time target: under 100ms (book cites Facebook typeahead article [1])
estimates: Per-prefix top-K cached at every trie node (space-for-time trade)
Browser / Cache-Control caching: max-age=3600 (book references Google's 1h cache)

client.name: Client (Browser / Mobile)
client.summary: Search box that fires an AJAX /search?q= on every keystroke and renders the top-5 dropdown. Browser caches responses for ~1h.

sections.heading: Per-keystroke requests (book §Back of the envelope)
sections.body: Book's explicit model: 'for every character entered into the search box, a client sends a request to the backend.' Typing 'dinner' sends 6 requests: q=d, q=di, q=din, q=dinn, q=dinne, q=dinner. 20 requests/query average.

sections.heading: AJAX (book §Query service)
sections.body: Requests are AJAX — they don't refresh the page. Browser renders results as each response lands.

sections.heading: Browser caching (book §Query service)
sections.body: Response includes `Cache-Control: private, max-age=3600`. Book: 'Google caches the results in the browser for 1 hour.' Subsequent requests for the same prefix within an hour are served from the browser cache — no backend hit.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: The client is the first line of defense. AJAX avoids page reloads; browser caching cuts repeat-prefix requests to zero for an hour; without these, backend QPS would balloon.

bottlenecks.title: Per-keystroke request storm overwhelming client network/battery
bottlenecks.trigger: Every keystroke fires an AJAX GET — typing 'dinner' sends 6 requests, and the design assumes ~20 requests per 20-char query. On flaky mobile networks (3G, high RTT) or under rapid typing, in-flight requests pile up faster than they return.
bottlenecks.symptom: Dropdown flickers or shows stale suggestions from an earlier prefix (out-of-order responses), noticeable input lag, elevated mobile battery/data usage complaints.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Debounce keystrokes (50–75ms), cancel in-flight XHR via AbortController when a newer keystroke fires, and tag each request with a monotonic sequence id so the renderer drops responses older than the currently displayed prefix.
bottlenecks.detection: Client RUM metric: ratio of (requests sent / keystrokes) should be <1 after debouncing; alert on p95 time-to-first-suggestion >150ms or on 'stale response discarded' counter spiking.

bottlenecks.title: Browser cache ineffective for long-tail prefixes
bottlenecks.trigger: Cache-Control max-age=3600 only helps on repeat prefixes within an hour. With 10 searches/user/day and diverse queries, most of the 20 per-keystroke requests per query are first-time prefixes for that user — cache hit ratio at the browser is low, so the 48K peak QPS backend assumption holds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Backend QPS tracks user typing volume almost 1:1; no QPS relief during traffic spikes; users on repeat sessions still see full round-trips for prefixes they've never typed before.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a client-side LRU of recent prefix→suggestions in localStorage/IndexedDB (keyed by prefix, TTL 1h) that survives tab reloads; additionally prefetch top-K for the first 1–2 characters on page load so early keystrokes are instant.
bottlenecks.detection: RUM metric: fraction of /search requests served from client storage vs network; alert if <20% for returning users, indicating the local cache layer is underperforming.

bottlenecks.title: Unicode / IME composition mishandling
bottlenecks.trigger: Base design is 'English lowercase only,' but real clients receive CJK IME composition events, emoji, accented chars. Firing a request per compositionupdate event can double or triple request volume and produce prefixes the server's ASCII-only trie cannot match.
bottlenecks.symptom: Empty dropdowns for non-Latin users, doubled request counts during IME composition, occasional 400s from the API's normalize step rejecting non-ASCII input.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Listen to `compositionend` (not `input`) for IME languages, normalize to NFC on the client before sending, and gate the request until the composed grapheme is complete. Align with the book's multi-language follow-up (Unicode trie nodes).
bottlenecks.detection: Log client-side: ratio of compositionupdate-to-compositionend events that triggered network requests; backend 400-rate on /search filtered by Accept-Language!= en.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client matters for autocomplete In most designs we treat the client as a dumb renderer, but for search autocomplete the browser is doing real systems work. The problem demands top-5 suggestions **within 100ms of every keystroke**, and the client is the thing that decides *when* to fire a request, *whether* to skip the network entirely, and *which* response to actually show the user. Typing "dinner" produces 6 keystrokes — if the client naively fires all 6 in parallel, responses can arrive out of order and the dropdown will flicker between prefixes. So the client debounces keystrokes (~50-75ms), cancels in-flight requests when a newer keystroke arrives, and tags requests with a sequence id to discard stale responses. ## What happens without it Without client-side logic, a user typing quickly on a flaky mobile connection sees the dropdown jump around as older responses land after newer ones, input feels laggy, and battery/data usage spikes. The backend also takes the hit: every keystroke becomes a real request, so the API tier and Trie Cache see their full theoretical load with no smoothing. ## The numbers The design assumes 10M DAU × 10 searches/day × 20 keystrokes/query = **2B requests/day, ~24K QPS average, ~48K peak**. The browser's `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` means if a user re-types the same prefix within an hour, it's served from browser cache — **zero backend hit**. On a 20-character query, even catching 20% of repeat prefixes shaves ~10K QPS off peak. ## Trade-off Pushing logic into the client means more JS complexity and inconsistent behavior across browsers, but it's the only place you can cut requests *before they leave the device*.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 LB routing /search requests to API servers.

sections.heading: Role (book Figure 13-11)
sections.body: Book step 1: 'A search query is sent to the load balancer.' Step 2: 'The load balancer routes the request to API servers.' Straightforward HTTP LB.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Round-robin with least-connections tie-break. Health-check path: GET /healthz.

sections.heading: TLS
sections.body: Terminate at LB; plaintext HTTP to API tier inside the VPC.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Stale-cache API replica: the LB can't tell, but stale data is still correct (just a bit outdated).
- Regional failure: serve from another region; browser cache for active users smooths the blip.

gained: Header-based routing for A/B trie versions

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU saturation at 48K peak QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: LB terminates TLS for all /search traffic. At 48K peak QPS with ~20 requests per typed query and mostly short-lived HTTPS connections from mobile clients, TLS handshakes (especially ECDHE+RSA) can dominate LB CPU if session resumption rates drop below ~90%.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegged at 95%+, p99 connection-establishment latency climbs from ~2ms to 50-200ms, pushing end-to-end past the 100ms SLO; sporadic TLS handshake timeouts on flaky mobile networks.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT resumption, provision session-ticket keys across LB fleet for cross-node resumption, prefer ECDSA certs over RSA (3-5x faster handshakes), and right-size LB fleet to keep per-node CPU under 60% at peak. Terminate HTTP/2 so one connection serves all 20 keystroke requests per query.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB CPU >70% sustained 5min, TLS handshakes/sec, and session-resumption hit ratio <85%. Track p99 of ssl_handshake_time metric; alert if >20ms.

bottlenecks.title: Connection concurrency ceiling from per-keystroke request pattern
bottlenecks.trigger: Sim config caps LB at 50K concurrent connections. Each user keystroke opens a request; with 10M DAU typing bursts and HTTP/1.1 clients (no multiplexing), connection counts can exceed concurrency cap during regional traffic spikes or when an upstream API replica slows and responses queue at the LB.
bottlenecks.symptom: New connections get TCP RST or queue in LB accept backlog; users see sporadic dropdown gaps where a keystroke request never returns; API replicas show normal latency but LB-side p99 spikes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 end-to-end so 20 keystroke requests/query share one connection (cuts connection count ~20x). Tune `net.core.somaxconn` and LB worker connection limits; add connection draining with 30s grace. Scale LB horizontally via DNS round-robin or anycast before hitting 70% of 50K cap per node.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor active_connections gauge and accept_queue_depth per LB node; alert at 70% of concurrency limit. Track HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 ratio — alert if HTTP/1.1 share grows unexpectedly.

bottlenecks.title: Regional LB failure with no client-side failover
bottlenecks.trigger: A single-region LB outage (AZ loss, misconfigured health checks, or control-plane issue) blackholes all in-flight /search traffic for that region. Browser cache (max-age=3600) only helps users who previously typed the exact same prefix; first-time prefixes during the outage all fail.
bottlenecks.symptom: Autocomplete dropdown empty or hangs for entire region of users; 5xx spike on LB access logs; users perceive search box as broken even though typed search still works (form POST to different endpoint).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy LBs in active-active across ≥2 regions with GeoDNS + health-based failover (Route53 or equivalent, TTL ≤60s). Client should gracefully hide the dropdown on network error rather than showing stale UI. Pre-warm backup region's Trie Cache so failover doesn't trigger mass cache-miss storm to Trie DB.
bottlenecks.detection: Synthetic probes from multiple geos hitting /healthz every 10s; alert on any region failing 2 consecutive probes. Track 5xx rate at LB; page on-call at >0.5% for 2min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Load Balancer for autocomplete Autocomplete is unusual because **every keystroke is a request**. Typing "dinner" fires 6 requests, and the design assumes ~20 requests per typed query across 10M users. That means the API tier can't be one big server — it has to be a fleet of stateless replicas, and *something* has to spread traffic across them while also terminating TLS at the edge. The load balancer is that something. It also gives us a single stable DNS name for the browser to hit, so we can add/remove API replicas without clients noticing. ## What happens without it If the browser hits one API server directly, a single replica restart (deploy, crash, AZ reboot) blackholes autocomplete for whichever users were pinned to it — their search box just hangs mid-type. The operator sees a partial outage that's invisible to global dashboards. Worse, you can't scale horizontally: the API tier is stateless precisely so you can throw more boxes at peak traffic, but without an LB there's no way to actually route to them. Health checks also disappear — a slow-GC'ing replica keeps receiving traffic it can't serve within the 100ms SLO. ## The number Peak is **48K QPS** of /search requests. If a single API replica handles ~2K QPS comfortably (given the 3–12ms service time and 5K concurrency budget), you need **~24 replicas at peak, ~48 for headroom**. The LB is what makes "24 boxes behave as one endpoint" possible. ## Trade-off You've added one network hop (~1–2ms) and a new failure domain in exchange for horizontal scalability and zero-downtime deploys — a trivially good trade at this scale.

api.name: API Servers
api.summary: Stateless service that fetches trie data from Trie Cache, constructs the top-5 suggestions, and returns. Also samples and emits the query to analytics logs.

sections.heading: Endpoint
sections.body:
```
GET /search?q=tr
→ { "suggestions": ["true", "try", "tree"] }
```

sections.heading: Lookup order (book Figure 13-11)
sections.body:
Book step 3: 'API servers get trie data from Trie Cache and construct autocomplete suggestions for the client.'
Step 4: 'In case the data is not in Trie Cache, we replenish data back to the cache' — i.e., on cache miss, fall through to Trie DB, then write back to cache.

sections.heading: Data sampling (book §Query service)
sections.body: Book: 'only 1 out of every N requests is logged by the system.' This keeps analytics log volume tractable at 48K peak QPS.

sections.heading: Response headers
sections.body: `Cache-Control: private, max-age=3600` — tells browser to cache for 1h (book references Google's behavior).

lost: Harder to tune ranking — ES weight model is coarse

bottlenecks.title: Trie Cache miss storm after weekly snapshot swap
bottlenecks.trigger: When the Trie Cache is swapped to a new weekly version (trie-2026-W17) or a cache shard restarts, the API's normal ~97% cache hit rate collapses. At 48K peak QPS, even a 20% miss rate pushes ~9.6K QPS of fall-through reads onto Trie DB (sim concurrency cap 2000), and each API request now waits 5–20ms on DB instead of 1–3ms on cache.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 /search latency jumps from ~15ms to 50–150ms, breaching the 100ms SLO; API concurrency (cap 5000) climbs as requests block on DB; Trie DB saturates and starts returning timeouts, causing 5xx bursts on the API tier right after every rebuild cycle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-warm the new Trie Cache generation before atomic swap: worker hydrates cache with top-N hottest prefixes (from aggregated_weekly) before flipping current_version. Add request coalescing (single-flight) in the API so concurrent misses for the same prefix issue one DB read. Cap DB fall-through with a per-API-replica semaphore and serve stale-from-old-cache on semaphore rejection.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on api.cache_hit_ratio < 0.90 for >30s, or triedb.qps > 2× baseline. Track p99 /search latency with a 100ms SLO burn-rate alert; page on sustained breach within 2min of a version bump.

bottlenecks.title: Synchronous analytics log emit blocking the hot path
bottlenecks.trigger: API emits sampled (query, ts) rows to Analytics Logs inline on every sampled request. At 48K peak QPS with 1:10 sampling, that's ~4.8K log writes/sec interleaved with the 3–12ms service budget. A log-tier hiccup (disk stall, Kafka broker rebalance, sim failureRate 0.0002) causes sampled requests to block on log append, tying up API worker slots (concurrency cap 5000).
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 latency bimodal — unsampled requests fast (~10ms), sampled ones slow (50–500ms); API goroutine/worker count climbs; occasional 5xx when log tier is flapping; log emit errors correlate 1:1 with user-facing latency spikes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Make the emit fully async: bounded in-memory ring buffer (e.g., 10K entries per replica) flushed by a background goroutine to Kafka with batching (100ms or 1KB). Drop-on-full with a counter rather than blocking the request path. Decouple sampling decision (cheap, inline) from transport (async).
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: api.log_emit_queue_depth and api.log_emit_dropped_total. Alert if dropped > 0.1% of sampled requests or queue_depth > 80% capacity. Track correlation between log-tier error rate and /search p99.

bottlenecks.title: Input normalization and validation CPU cost at 48K QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: Every keystroke request hits API's normalize (lowercase, ASCII-check, length cap per book's 50-char limit, shard_map lookup). At 48K peak QPS with ~20 req/query from 10M DAU, a regex-heavy or allocation-heavy normalize path burns measurable CPU per replica. Non-ASCII input (IME, emoji) hits the slow/reject path, amplifying cost and producing 400s.
bottlenecks.symptom: API CPU saturation before cache/DB becomes a bottleneck; per-replica throughput plateaus well below the 5000 concurrency budget; elevated 400 rate from non-English users; horizontal scaling cost grows linearly with keystroke volume rather than query volume.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Precompile regexes at startup; use byte-level ASCII fast-path with fallback to Unicode NFC only when high bit set; cache shard_map lookups in a per-replica LRU (prefixes are heavily Zipf-distributed). Enforce max prefix length (50 chars, per book) early with a cheap len-check before allocation. Move reject-on-invalid to LB via WAF rule to shed bad traffic before API CPU.
bottlenecks.detection: Profile-based alert: api.cpu_pct > 60% sustained at steady QPS; track api.normalize_p99_us (target <200µs). Alert on 400-rate > 0.5% segmented by Accept-Language to catch Unicode regressions.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the API tier exists here For a search autocomplete system that must return top-5 suggestions in under 100ms, *something* has to sit between the browser and the Trie Cache and do the unglamorous glue work: parse `?q=tr`, normalize the string (lowercase, length-cap, ASCII check), look up which shard owns that prefix, call the cache, fall through to the Trie DB on a miss, run the result through the filter layer, attach the `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` header, and sample the query into analytics logs. You can't expose the Trie Cache directly to the internet — it has no auth, no input validation, no sampling, and no opinion about which shard to ask. The API tier is where all of that policy lives, and keeping it **stateless** is what lets you scale it horizontally behind the load balancer. ## What breaks without it Without an API layer, a malformed query (`q=` with 10KB of emoji) hits the cache directly and either crashes a shard or pollutes it. The filter layer never runs, so banned suggestions leak to users between rebuild cycles. Analytics logs go dark, which means the next weekly trie rebuild has no fresh frequency data — trending queries never surface. Operators see cache-shard instability and a stale top-K; users see garbage suggestions. ## The number Peak load is **48K QPS** (10M DAU × 10 searches × 20 keystrokes ÷ 86400 × 2). With a per-replica budget of ~2K QPS at 3–12ms service time, you need **~24 API replicas at peak** — only possible because the tier is stateless and identical. ## Trade-off You've added one network hop (~5ms) in exchange for a place to enforce policy, sample traffic, and scale independently of the cache.

filter.name: Filter Layer
filter.summary: Filters out hateful, violent, sexually explicit, or dangerous autocomplete suggestions before they reach the client. Book §Trie operations / Delete.

sections.heading: Role (book §Delete, Figure 13-14)
sections.body: Book places a filter 'in front of the Trie Cache to filter out unwanted suggestions. Having a filter layer gives us the flexibility of removing results based on different filter rules.'

sections.heading: Two-stage cleanup
sections.body:
- Online: filter layer strips banned suggestions from every response (fast, rule-based).
- Offline: unwanted suggestions are 'removed physically from the database asynchronically so the correct data set will be used to build trie in the next update cycle.' Both stages run — the filter catches leaks between rebuild cycles.

sections.heading: Rule sources
sections.body: Blocklist regexes, model-classifier scores, region-specific policies. Rules update independently of the trie rebuild — you don't have to rebuild the whole trie to ban a newly flagged phrase.

alternatives.name: Inline filter at the API layer (no separate component)

lost: Rules are coupled to API deploy cycle — slower to ship a takedown

bottlenecks.title: Regex rule-set evaluation cost scales with blocklist size at 48K QPS
bottlenecks.trigger: Filter runs every rule against every top-5 suggestion on every request. At 48K peak QPS × 5 candidates = 240K suggestion-checks/sec. As trust-and-safety adds regional rules (thousands of regex patterns for hate/violent/NSFW across languages), per-request CPU cost grows linearly and the 1–3ms sim budget blows out.
bottlenecks.symptom: Filter p99 climbs from ~2ms to 20–50ms, pushing end-to-end past the 100ms SLO; CPU saturation on filter nodes before concurrency cap (50K) is reached; autocomplete feels laggy right after a bulk rule import.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Compile all regex patterns into a single Aho-Corasick / Hyperscan multi-pattern automaton (O(n) in suggestion length regardless of rule count). Partition rules by region and only load the active region's set per request. Cache filter verdicts per (prefix, rule-set-version) in a per-replica LRU since prefixes are Zipf-distributed.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: filter.eval_time_us p99 (alert >5ms), filter.rules_loaded gauge, and filter.cpu_pct. Alert on CPU >60% sustained 5min or p99 breaching 5ms after any rule-store publish event.

bottlenecks.title: Rule-store publish storm causing stale or inconsistent takedowns
bottlenecks.trigger: Takedown flow (operation 'takedown') relies on filter rules taking effect 'sub-minute' across all filter replicas. With the filter fronting every /search at 48K QPS across many replicas and regions, a naive poll-based rule refresh (e.g., every 30s) means replicas briefly disagree — some strip the term, some don't — for up to the poll interval after a high-priority takedown.
bottlenecks.symptom: Trust team reports the banned term still appears in autocomplete for some users minutes after takedown; support tickets cite inconsistent behavior across sessions/regions; audit logs show mixed rule-version IDs serving traffic concurrently.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Push-based rule distribution via a pub/sub channel (Redis pub/sub, etcd watch, or Kafka compacted topic) so all replicas converge in <1s. Include a monotonic rule_version in every response header for observability; block deploys/restarts until replica catches up to latest version. Add an emergency 'kill-switch' fast path that bypasses regex compile for literal-string takedowns.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: filter.rule_version_lag_seconds per replica (alert >5s), and a distribution of rule_version across the fleet (alert if >1 distinct version for >10s). Synthetic canary query that checks a known test-takedown term is filtered within 2s of publish.

bottlenecks.title: Filter failure mode: fail-open leaks banned content, fail-closed breaks autocomplete
bottlenecks.trigger: Filter sits in the hot path of every suggest response. If the filter tier degrades (rule-store unreachable, Hyperscan OOM, deploy bug), the API must choose: fail-open (return unfiltered top-K) or fail-closed (return empty / 5xx). Sim failureRate 0.0001 × 48K QPS ≈ 5 failures/sec baseline; a partial outage amplifies this.
bottlenecks.symptom: Fail-open path: banned/NSFW suggestions briefly leak to users, producing PR/legal incidents. Fail-closed path: autocomplete dropdown goes empty globally, looking like a total outage even though search itself works.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tiered fallback: (1) primary filter tier with Hyperscan; (2) degraded local filter in the API process running only a small hard-coded 'critical banlist' (top ~500 terms) so even total filter-tier failure still blocks the worst content; (3) circuit-breaker in API with 50ms timeout to filter, falling through to tier-2 on breach. Never fail-open on unchecked content.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: filter.circuit_breaker_open_total, filter.timeout_rate (alert >0.1%), and api.degraded_filter_path_used counter. Alert if the degraded path serves >1% of traffic for >1min, and page on any filter.timeout_rate spike >1% for 30s.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a filter layer for autocomplete For a search autocomplete system, the top-5 suggestions are **precomputed weekly** and cached in the trie. That cadence is the whole reason this design is fast — but it also means the serving path has no opinion about *what* it's serving. If a term goes viral for ugly reasons on Monday, it sits in the trie until the next Sunday rebuild. Worse, autocomplete is uniquely sensitive: unlike search results (which respond to an explicit query), suggestions are *proactively surfaced* to users mid-keystroke, so a hateful or NSFW completion gets put in front of someone who never asked for it. The filter layer is the online escape hatch that lets trust-and-safety ship a takedown in seconds instead of waiting a week for the next trie build. ## What happens without it A term gets flagged Monday morning. Without the filter, the only way to remove it is to delete it from `aggregated_weekly` and wait for Sunday's rebuild — six days of the term appearing under every matching prefix. Users screenshot the dropdown, press coverage follows, and the operator's only lever is an emergency trie rebuild (hours of pipeline runtime) or manually poking cache entries across every shard. ## The number At **48K peak QPS × 5 candidates per response = 240K suggestion-checks/sec**, the filter has to be cheap — a few hundred microseconds per request — to stay inside the 100ms end-to-end SLO. That's why it's rule-based (regex/Aho-Corasick) rather than a model call. ## Trade-off You've added a hop and a rule store to decouple takedown latency from rebuild cadence — correctness at the cost of one more thing to operate.

cache.name: Trie Cache
cache.summary: Distributed cache holding the trie (or per-prefix top-K) in memory for fast read. Takes weekly snapshots of Trie DB.

sections.heading: Role (book §Trie Cache)
sections.body: Book: 'Trie Cache is a distributed cache system that keeps trie in memory for fast read. It takes a weekly snapshot of the DB.' Each API request reads from this cache.

sections.heading: Why cache if trie is on disk
sections.body: The trie can be millions of nodes. Going to the Trie DB (document store or KV) on every keystroke adds disk I/O — caching the trie (or hot prefixes) in RAM keeps the read path sub-millisecond. Matches book's §Query service §Lookup order — DB is only hit on cache miss.

sections.heading: Sharding (book §Scale the storage)
sections.body: Naive: shard by first character ('a-m' on server 1, 'n-z' on server 2); but 'c' has many more words than 'x' → imbalance. Book's solution: shard map manager analyses historical distribution and maintains a lookup DB ('one shard for 's', another for 'u-z').

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Cache server out-of-memory or offline → fall through to Trie DB (book §Query service step 4).
- Cache restart: cold until first reads hydrate hot prefixes from DB.

lost: No persistence → lost on restart; no atomic multi-key version swap

gained: Book §Wrap-up: 'we can store tries in CDNs' for per-country top queries
lost: Invalidation across edge PoPs is slow (minutes)

bottlenecks.title: Cold cache after weekly snapshot swap triggers thundering herd to Trie DB
bottlenecks.trigger: Weekly trie rebuild atomically swaps cache to trie-2026-W17; the new generation starts empty (or with cold pages) while 48K peak QPS of /search keeps flowing. Every prefix miss falls through to Trie DB (sim concurrency cap 2000, 5–20ms service time), and because hot prefixes are Zipf-distributed, thousands of concurrent requests for the same prefix all miss simultaneously.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 /search latency spikes from ~3ms (cache hit) to 50–200ms for minutes after swap; Trie DB saturates its 2000 concurrency budget and starts returning timeouts; API tier concurrency climbs as requests block on DB; 100ms SLO breached globally right after every Sunday rebuild.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-warm the new cache generation before flipping current_version: worker hydrates the top-N hottest prefixes (from aggregated_weekly frequency column) into the new snapshot, then atomically swaps. Add single-flight/request-coalescing in the API so concurrent misses for the same prefix issue one DB read. Keep the old generation resident for a grace period so in-flight reads drain without falling through.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: cache.hit_ratio per version (alert <0.90 for >30s post-swap); triedb.qps (alert >2× baseline); cache.version_swap_event correlated with p99 /search latency. Dashboard burn-rate alert on 100ms SLO within 2min of any version bump.

bottlenecks.title: Shard hotspotting on popular prefix buckets despite shard-map rebalance
bottlenecks.trigger: Shard map groups prefixes by historical volume, but a viral event (e.g., breaking news, trending celebrity) causes one prefix bucket — say 's' — to absorb a disproportionate share of the 48K peak QPS. Since the shard map only updates on the weekly rebuild cadence, the hot shard has no relief for up to a week. Sim concurrency cap per cache node is 10K, so a shard taking >10K QPS queues requests.
bottlenecks.symptom: One cache shard's CPU and network pegged at 95%+ while peers idle; p99 latency for prefixes on that shard climbs to 20–50ms while other prefixes stay at 2ms; uneven API replica latency depending on which shard they hit; potential shard OOM if top-K payloads for the hot prefix are replicated across too many API-side request buffers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replicate hot shards across multiple cache nodes (N=3) with client-side randomized read among replicas; detect hot prefixes in real-time via a sampling counter on cache nodes and publish replica hints to API shard-map cache (TTL 60s). Add a local per-API-replica LRU of the top ~1000 prefixes (Zipf tail is tiny) to absorb hot reads before they ever hit the cache tier.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard metrics: cache.shard_qps, cache.shard_cpu_pct, cache.shard_p99_ms. Alert if any shard's QPS exceeds 2× fleet median for >2min, or if shard_cpu_pct >70% sustained. Track top-K hottest prefixes per minute; alert on sudden rank changes indicating viral traffic.

bottlenecks.title: Memory footprint blow-up from top-K stored at every trie node
bottlenecks.trigger: Design caches top-5 (query, freq) pairs at every trie node to make online lookup O(1). With ~10M distinct queries × avg 20 chars = ~30M trie nodes, each holding top-5 × ~25B/entry ≈ 125B of top-K plus node overhead ≈ 200–300B per node → ~6–9 GB per trie generation per shard replica. Multi-language (Unicode nodes) or per-country tries multiply this further.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cache nodes approaching memory limits trigger evictions of cold prefixes, forcing Trie DB fall-through for long-tail queries; during swap, both old and new generations resident simultaneously doubles RAM need and can OOM the node; GC/compaction pauses on cache nodes cause sporadic 10–50ms latency spikes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use compressed trie representations (radix tree / DAWG) to collapse shared suffixes; intern query strings across top-K entries (hot queries like 'facebook' appear in top-K of many ancestor nodes). Store top-K as varint-encoded ids into a side string table rather than raw strings. Size cache nodes at ≥2× single-generation footprint to safely hold both versions during swap. Consider tiered cache: hot prefixes (first 1–2 chars) fully in RAM, deeper prefixes memory-mapped from local SSD.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: cache.memory_used_bytes, cache.evictions_per_sec (baseline should be ~0; alert on any sustained eviction rate), cache.gc_pause_p99_ms. Capacity-plan alert at 70% of node RAM; forecast growth from aggregated_weekly row count trend.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Trie Cache is here For a search autocomplete system that promises top-5 suggestions in **under 100ms per keystroke**, the Trie Cache is what makes the math work. The trie itself — millions of nodes, each holding a precomputed top-5 for its prefix — lives durably in the Trie DB (MongoDB or a KV store). But disk reads are 5–20ms each, and every keystroke is a separate request. Serving 48K peak QPS off disk would blow the latency budget before the response even left the API server. The cache holds the trie (or the hot prefix → top-K map) in RAM so the lookup is a ~1–3ms memory read. ## What happens without it Drop the cache and every `/search?q=tr` keystroke hits the Trie DB directly. With the DB sim'd at 2000 concurrent requests and 5–20ms service time, it saturates almost instantly at peak load. Users see the dropdown lag behind their typing — suggestions appear *after* they've moved on to the next character — and the dropdown feels broken. Operators see Trie DB pegged at 100% CPU, API replicas piling up in-flight requests against their 5000 concurrency limit, and a cascading latency spike across the whole serving path. ## The number Peak is **48K QPS** (10M DAU × 10 searches × 20 keystrokes ÷ 86400 × 2). At a 97% cache hit rate, only ~1.4K QPS fall through to the Trie DB — comfortably inside its 2000 concurrency budget. Without the cache, all 48K QPS hit the DB: **24× over capacity**. ## Trade-off You're accepting weekly snapshot staleness and RAM cost in exchange for sub-millisecond reads — the freshness gap is what the filter layer and stream-rebuild follow-up exist to patch.

triedb.name: Trie DB (persistent)
triedb.summary: Durable storage of the serialized trie. Book considers two options: document store (MongoDB) or hash-table-form KV store.

sections.heading: Option 1: Document store (book §Trie DB)
sections.body: Book: 'Since a new trie is built weekly, we can periodically take a snapshot of it, serialize it, and store the serialized data in the database. Document stores like MongoDB are good fits for serialized data.'

sections.heading: Option 2: Hash-table form KV store (book §Trie DB)
sections.body:
'A trie can be represented in a hash table form by applying the following logic:
- Every prefix in the trie is mapped to a key in a hash table.
- Data on each trie node is mapped to a value in a hash table.'
```
'tr' → {children: ['e','y','u'], topK: [('true',35),('try',29),('tree',10)]}
'tre' → {children: ['e'], topK: [('tree',10)]}
```

sections.heading: Access pattern
sections.body: Written in bulk by workers every rebuild cycle. Read by Trie Cache on misses and warm-up. Low-QPS store — most reads are absorbed by the cache tier.

sections.heading: Sharding
sections.body: Same shard map as the cache (managed by the shard-map manager) so a prefix lives on co-located cache+DB shards — minimizes cross-shard traffic on a cache miss.

gained: Natural fit for serialized trie blobs
lost: Per-prefix read needs blob load + walk vs hash-table direct lookup

gained: Book's second option: O(1) prefix lookup
lost: Storage overhead per prefix (vs shared trie structure)

bottlenecks.title: Cache-miss fall-through saturates Trie DB after weekly snapshot swap
bottlenecks.trigger: Right after the weekly rebuild atomically swaps Trie Cache to trie-2026-W17, the new generation is cold. At 48K peak QPS, even a 20% miss rate pushes ~9.6K QPS of reads into Trie DB, which is sim'd at only 2000 concurrency with 5–20ms service time — a ~5x overload. Zipf-distributed hot prefixes make thousands of concurrent misses pile on the same keys.
bottlenecks.symptom: Trie DB p99 latency spikes from ~15ms to hundreds of ms or timeouts; API request concurrency climbs toward its 5000 cap as requests block on DB reads; end-to-end /search p99 breaches the 100ms SLO for minutes after every Sunday swap; 5xx bursts visible on API tier.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-warm the new Trie Cache generation before flipping current_version — worker hydrates top-N hottest prefixes (ranked by aggregated_weekly.frequency) directly into cache so the swap is already warm. Keep the previous generation resident during a grace window so in-flight reads drain. Add single-flight/request-coalescing at the API so concurrent misses for the same prefix issue one DB read. Rate-limit DB fall-through per API replica with a semaphore, serving stale-from-old-cache on rejection.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on triedb.qps > 2x baseline (e.g., >3K QPS sustained for 30s), triedb.concurrency_used > 70% of 2000 cap, or triedb.p99_ms > 40ms. Correlate with cache.version_swap events — burn-rate alert on the 100ms /search SLO within 2min of any version bump.

bottlenecks.title: Bulk weekly write amplification during trie publish
bottlenecks.trigger: Each weekly rebuild writes the entire serialized trie (~30M prefix rows × ~200–300B per entry ≈ 6–9 GB per shard, growing ~0.4 GB/day per book's estimate) in a tight window. If writes go to the same shards that are simultaneously serving cache-miss reads, write I/O contends with read I/O — worsened by MongoDB's doc-level locks or KV-store compactions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Read p99 climbs during the publish window; cache-miss reads that normally complete in 5–20ms stretch to 100ms+; compaction backlogs or replication lag visible on Trie DB; operators see the rebuild job taking longer week over week as data grows.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Write to a new version namespace (triedb.v=2026-W17) rather than mutating current rows, then flip a pointer atomically — decouples write traffic from read traffic and makes rollback trivial. Throttle the worker's bulk-write rate (e.g., cap at 20% of DB IOPS budget) and schedule the publish during the region's low-traffic window. Use bulk/batch APIs (Mongo bulkWrite, KV store multi-put) to amortize per-row overhead.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: triedb.write_iops, triedb.compaction_backlog_bytes, and triedb.replication_lag_seconds during publish windows. Alert if read p99 during publish is >2x the non-publish baseline, or if publish duration exceeds 2 hours (leading indicator of scale tipping).

bottlenecks.title: Shard hotspotting from prefix skew outpaces weekly shard-map updates
bottlenecks.trigger: Shard Map Manager rebalances only on the weekly rebuild cadence. A mid-week viral event (trending celebrity, breaking news) concentrates cache-miss reads onto one prefix bucket — e.g., 's' — and the hot shard's 2000 concurrency budget is swamped while peer shards idle. Co-location of cache+DB shards means a hot cache shard drives a hot DB shard.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Trie DB shard shows CPU/IOPS at 90%+ while peers sit at 10%; p99 latency for any prefix routed to the hot shard spikes to 50–100ms; localized 5xx / timeouts bound to a subset of prefixes; no relief until next Sunday's rebuild publishes a new shard map.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replicate hot shards with N=3 read replicas and let API clients randomize across replicas; publish runtime hotspot hints (TTL 60s) so the shard-map manager can react mid-week rather than weekly. Add a per-API-replica LRU of top ~1K prefix→top-K entries (Zipf tail is tiny) to absorb hot reads before they reach the DB. For emergencies, support manual shard-map override that takes effect without a full rebuild.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard metrics: triedb.shard_qps, triedb.shard_cpu_pct, triedb.shard_p99_ms. Alert if any shard's QPS exceeds 2x fleet median for >2min, or shard_cpu_pct >70% sustained. Monitor top-K hottest prefixes per minute; page if rank churn indicates an unexpected viral shift.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Trie DB is here For a search autocomplete system that rebuilds its trie weekly from a billion-plus log rows, the worker spends hours computing the top-5 suggestions for every prefix — and that result has to live *somewhere durable*. The Trie Cache holds the trie in RAM for speed, but RAM is volatile: a cache node restart, a deploy, or an AZ reboot would wipe the whole precomputed structure, and you can't afford to re-run the weekly batch job just because one cache box rebooted. The Trie DB is the durable record of "what the trie looks like this week" — the cache reads from it on cold-start and on per-prefix misses. ## What happens without it Drop the Trie DB and every cache restart becomes a catastrophe: the cache comes up empty, has nothing to fall through to, and serves empty dropdowns until the next weekly rebuild finishes — potentially days of broken autocomplete. Users see no suggestions; the operator sees the cache-miss counter at 100% with nowhere for those misses to go; the worker pipeline becomes a single point of failure for serving, not just for freshness. ## The number With ~10M distinct queries and top-5 cached at every trie node (~30M nodes × ~200B), you're persisting roughly **6–9 GB per trie generation**. At the book's **0.4 GB/day** growth of new queries, that's a slow-moving dataset — perfect for a document store or KV where writes are bulk-weekly and reads are rare (only ~3% cache-miss fall-through at 48K peak QPS ≈ 1.4K QPS). ## Trade-off You've accepted an extra storage tier and a 5–20ms miss penalty in exchange for surviving cache restarts without a week-long outage.

shardmap.name: Shard Map Manager
shardmap.summary: Maintains the prefix → shard lookup to balance load across storage/cache shards. Book §Scale the storage, Figure 13-15.

sections.heading: Why we need it (book §Scale the storage)
sections.body: Naive first-character sharding ('a-m' vs 'n-z') is imbalanced: 'there are a lot more words that start with the letter c than x.' So we analyze historical distribution and group letters with similar volume together: one shard for 's', one for 'u-z', etc.

sections.heading: Lookup DB
sections.body: Book: 'The shard map manager maintains a lookup database for identifying where rows should be stored.' API asks 'where does prefix tr live?' before reading. Typically an in-memory map loaded at process start.

sections.heading: Resharding
sections.body: When distribution drifts (new language, viral term), shard map is updated and worker publishes a new trie layout. Online path reads the new map on next refresh.

gained: No central map — hash function gives the shard
lost: Can't compensate for real-world skew (most-popular prefixes are not random)

bottlenecks.title: Stale shard map during mid-week viral traffic shifts
bottlenecks.trigger: Shard map is recomputed only on the weekly rebuild cadence, but prefix distribution can shift within hours (breaking news, viral celebrity, product launch). At 48K peak QPS, a single prefix bucket like 's' can absorb 2x+ fleet-median load while the map still reflects last week's balanced layout.
bottlenecks.symptom: One cache+DB shard pair CPU-pegged at 90%+ while peers idle; p99 /search latency for affected prefixes climbs from ~3ms to 20–50ms, breaching the 100ms SLO for a subset of users; no relief possible without a manual intervention until Sunday's rebuild.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Publish runtime hotspot hints with a TTL of 60s derived from per-shard QPS telemetry, and allow the shard map manager to spawn ephemeral replica shards for hot prefixes without waiting for a full trie rebuild. Support a manual override API so on-call can repin a hot prefix bucket to a dedicated shard mid-week.
bottlenecks.detection: Track shardmap.prefix_qps_skew_ratio (max shard QPS / median shard QPS); alert if >2.0 sustained for 2min. Alert on per-shard cache.shard_cpu_pct >70% when fleet median is <40%, indicating the map is no longer balancing real traffic.

bottlenecks.title: Shard map lookup as a hot-path dependency for every /search
bottlenecks.trigger: Every API request calls shardmap.shard_for(prefix) before reading cache/DB. At 48K peak QPS × ~24 API replicas, that's ~2K lookups/sec per replica against the lookup DB. If the lookup is a remote call (rather than an in-memory map loaded at startup), shard map manager availability becomes a single point of failure for the entire read path.
bottlenecks.symptom: Shard map unavailability → every /search fails because API can't decide which shard to query; 5xx rate spikes to 100% across the fleet within seconds; cache and DB are healthy but unreachable because nobody knows their addresses.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Load the shard map into each API replica at startup as an in-memory map (refreshed every 60s via background pull); never block a request on a remote shard map call. Cache the last-known-good map to local disk so a replica restart during a shard-map-manager outage still serves traffic with a slightly stale layout.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: api.shardmap_lookup_source (in-memory vs remote) — alert on any remote lookups in steady state. Track api.shardmap_age_seconds per replica; alert if >300s, indicating the refresh pipeline is broken and map is drifting toward staleness.

bottlenecks.title: Inconsistent shard map versions across cache, DB, and API during reshard publish
bottlenecks.trigger: When the shard map manager publishes a new mapping (e.g., splitting 'c' into its own shard), API replicas, Trie Cache nodes, and Trie DB shards all refresh independently. During the propagation window (seconds to minutes, depending on refresh cadence), an API might ask cache v2 for a prefix that cache still thinks belongs to shard v1, or write back a miss to the wrong shard.
bottlenecks.symptom: Elevated cache-miss rate right after a reshard publish (hit ratio drops from 0.97 to 0.80+); some prefixes served from two shards simultaneously with divergent top-K; occasional 'prefix not found' errors on Trie DB reads that hit the wrong shard; operators see confusing logs where the same prefix routes differently across requests.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Version the shard map and include shard_map_version in every cache/DB request; reject reads with a mismatched version and fall through to the coordinator to resolve. Use a two-phase rollout: (1) dual-publish to old and new shards for a grace window, (2) flip API to read from new map only after telemetry confirms all cache/DB nodes have converged on the new version.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: shardmap.version_skew (count of distinct versions observed across fleet); alert if >1 version persists for >30s after a publish. Track cache.version_mismatch_total and triedb.wrong_shard_read_total; alert on any nonzero rate outside a publish window.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Shard Map Manager for autocomplete The trie for this system is huge — roughly 30M nodes holding top-5 suggestions for every prefix, totaling 6–9 GB per generation. That's too big for one cache or DB box, so we split it across shards. The obvious way to shard is by first letter: "a–m" on one box, "n–z" on another. But English prefixes are wildly skewed — there are vastly more queries starting with "c" or "s" than with "x" or "z". A naive split means one shard melts while its neighbor idles. The Shard Map Manager exists to fix exactly this: it analyzes real query distribution and groups letters so each shard carries roughly equal load ("s" gets its own shard, "u–z" share one, etc.). ## What happens without it With dumb first-letter sharding, the "s" shard at peak hits maybe 3× its fair share of the 48K QPS, saturates its 10K concurrency cap, and returns slow responses or timeouts. Users typing anything starting with common letters see the 100ms SLO blown, while operators stare at dashboards showing half the cache fleet idle. The API tier can't route around it — it has no idea *which* shard owns which prefix without this lookup. ## The number At **48K peak QPS** spread across, say, 8 shards, balanced load is ~6K QPS/shard. If first-letter sharding sends 30% of traffic to the "c" shard, that's **14.4K QPS on one box** — 44% over its 10K concurrency budget. ## Trade-off You've added a small coordination layer and one lookup per request in exchange for avoiding hot shards that no amount of hardware can paper over.

logs.name: Analytics Logs
logs.summary: Append-only, unindexed log of raw search queries. Book §Data gathering service.

sections.heading: Role (book §Analytics Logs)
sections.body: Book: 'It stores raw data about search queries. Logs are append-only and are not indexed.' Sample row: (query, time) — e.g. ('tree', 2019-10-01 22:01:01).

sections.heading: Write source
sections.body: API servers emit a log row for each (possibly sampled) request. Given 1:N sampling (book §Data sampling), ~4.8K rows/sec hit the log even at peak 48K QPS.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: Hot log retained long enough for the aggregator to process (days to a week); older rows archived to object storage.

gained: Book §Wrap-up mentions Kafka for real-time extension
lost: More ops than a flat append-only log
Shard-based billing; ordering per shard not per partition-key

bottlenecks.title: Write throughput saturation from per-keystroke request logging
bottlenecks.trigger: At 48K peak QPS with 20 requests per typed query, unsampled logging would drive 48K rows/sec of appends. Even with the book's 1:N sampling (e.g., 1:10 → ~4.8K rows/sec; 1:1 worst case → 48K rows/sec), a single append-only log file or unpartitioned Kafka topic with default partition count (~3-6) cannot sustain that write rate — each partition tops out around 10-50MB/s and a single broker leader becomes the chokepoint.
bottlenecks.symptom: API servers see log-emit latency climb from ~2-8ms into hundreds of ms, back-pressuring the hot /search path and breaching the 100ms SLO; Kafka producer buffers fill and start dropping or blocking; disk write queues on log brokers spike; downstream aggregator falls behind because upstream ingestion is throttled.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Partition the Kafka topic by hash(query) into ≥32 partitions so writes fan out across brokers; use async producers with batching (linger.ms=20, batch.size=64KB) and acks=1 on the hot path; enforce sampling at the API tier (1:10 default, configurable) so steady-state is ~4.8K rows/sec; isolate log-emit failures from the request path with a bounded in-memory queue that drops on overflow rather than blocking.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on producer.record-send-rate vs broker.bytes-in-per-sec divergence (indicates buffering); alert on api.log_emit_p99_ms > 20ms or api.log_emit_dropped_total > 0.5% sampled requests; track per-partition bytes-in skew — alert if max/median > 3x indicating hot-partition.

bottlenecks.title: Storage growth outpacing retention window
bottlenecks.trigger: Book's estimate is ~0.4 GB/day of new query data at 20% new-query rate, but raw logs capture all sampled requests including repeats. At 4.8K rows/sec × ~40 bytes/row (query + ts + metadata) ≈ 16 GB/day raw, or ~112 GB per weekly aggregation window. Without tiering, hot log storage grows unbounded and the aggregator's weekly scan gets slower each cycle.
bottlenecks.symptom: Aggregator job runtime grows week over week (from hours to eventually exceeding the weekly cadence); hot log disk utilization on Kafka brokers crosses 80% triggering retention-policy evictions that race with aggregator reads; stale data risk if aggregator can't finish before trie rebuild deadline, leading to a skipped weekly refresh.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set Kafka retention.ms to 10 days (slightly longer than the weekly aggregation window) and retention.bytes as a hard ceiling per partition; tier older segments to S3/object storage via Kafka Tiered Storage or a Kafka Connect sink; compress log payload with zstd (typical 4-5x ratio on query text); archive raw logs older than one rebuild cycle to cold storage for compliance only.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor kafka.log.size per partition with alert at 70% of retention.bytes; track aggregator job duration trend — alert if this-week duration > 1.3× 4-week moving average; alert on any retention-based eviction happening before the aggregator's last-read offset.

bottlenecks.title: Sampling bias distorting trie top-K rankings
bottlenecks.trigger: Book §Data sampling says only 1 of every N requests is logged to keep volume tractable at 48K peak QPS. Naive uniform sampling under-represents long-tail queries (a query appearing 10 times/week might be sampled 0 or 1 times at N=10), and geographic/temporal bursts get flattened. With ~20% of daily queries being new, a fresh trending query may not accumulate enough samples to surface in top-5 at any prefix.
bottlenecks.symptom: Trending/viral queries missing from autocomplete suggestions even a week after going viral; top-K for popular prefixes looks stable-but-stale; product team reports 'autocomplete doesn't know about X' for queries with meaningful real volume; A/B tests show suggestion click-through rate lags expected based on query-log analysis.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use stratified sampling: always log 100% of queries with frequency < threshold (bucketed via a Count-Min Sketch on the API tier) and down-sample only head traffic; alternatively, emit HyperLogLog / CMS counters in addition to raw rows so the aggregator can reconstruct true frequencies without relying on sample counts; keep full (unsampled) logs for a shorter window (24h) for trending detection path.
bottlenecks.detection: Periodic audit job comparing sampled-log-derived frequency to unsampled-counter frequency for a holdout set of queries — alert if estimation error >15% on the top 1000 queries; track coverage metric: fraction of queries in aggregated_weekly with frequency >= 5 that appeared in ≥3 distinct sample windows.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Analytics Logs are here For a search autocomplete system, the whole trick is that the trie already knows the top-5 suggestions for every prefix *before* the user types. But "top-5" only means something if you know which queries are popular — and that popularity signal has to come from somewhere. Analytics Logs are the raw record of what people actually searched for. Without them, the Trie Build Workers have nothing to rank by, and the weekly rebuild can't distinguish "facebook" (900M hits) from "facetious" (a few thousand). The log is the bridge between what users *do* and what the system *suggests*. ## What happens without it If the API just served a precomputed trie with no feedback loop, the suggestions would freeze at whatever the engineering team seeded on day one. Trending queries ("world cup," a viral celebrity name) never surface. Users notice the dropdown feels stale; the product team has no data to tune ranking; the Aggregators and downstream Aggregated Data table sit empty, so the weekly worker job either skips or produces the same trie every week. ## The number At 48K peak QPS, logging every request unsampled would be ~48K rows/sec. The book's 1:N sampling (say 1:10) brings that to ~4.8K rows/sec — roughly 16 GB/day of raw log, which a partitioned Kafka topic absorbs comfortably while still giving the Aggregators enough signal to rank ~10M distinct queries per week. ## Trade-off You've accepted that suggestions lag real user behavior by up to a week in exchange for a dead-simple, cheap batch pipeline instead of streaming infrastructure.

agg.name: Aggregators
agg.summary: Batch (or micro-batch) jobs that roll raw log rows up into (query, time-window, frequency) aggregates. Book §Aggregators.

sections.heading: Role (book §Aggregators)
sections.body: Book: 'The size of analytics logs is usually very large, and data is not in the right format. We need to aggregate data so it can be easily processed by our system.'

sections.heading: Cadence
sections.body: Depends on use case. Book: 'For real-time applications such as Twitter, we aggregate data in a shorter time interval… aggregating data less frequently, say once per week, might be good enough for many use cases.' Base design: weekly.

sections.heading: Output schema
sections.body:
```
TABLE aggregated_weekly query TEXT time TIMESTAMP (week start) frequency BIGINT PRIMARY KEY (query, time)
```

gained: Book real-time path: Spark Streaming / Storm / Kafka for near-real-time trending queries
lost: Stateful windowing is harder to operate than nightly batch

gained: Book references Hadoop MapReduce in the real-time discussion
lost: Higher latency than Spark; only OK when weekly cadence is acceptable

bottlenecks.title: Weekly batch job runtime outgrowing the rebuild window
bottlenecks.trigger: Aggregator must process ~1.4B sampled log rows/week (4.8K rows/sec × 7 days at 1:10 sampling of the 48K peak QPS stream) and group-by ~10M distinct queries into (query, week, frequency). With sim service times of 100–2000ms per task and concurrency cap of 50, a naive single-stage shuffle on ~28 GB/week of raw logs can stretch past the Sunday rebuild deadline as data grows 0.4 GB/day.
bottlenecks.symptom: Trie Build Workers start before aggregated_weekly is fully populated, producing a trie missing recent queries; or the weekly rebuild slips hours/days, leaving Trie Cache serving last-week's top-K beyond the intended cadence; on-call sees Spark/MapReduce job duration trending upward week over week.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use Spark with ≥200 partitions on hash(query), pre-aggregate with a Count-Min Sketch or combiner on the map side to collapse hot queries (Zipf tail shrinks shuffle volume 10×+), and checkpoint intermediate (query, day, frequency) rollups daily so the weekly job only merges 7 daily aggregates instead of re-scanning raw logs. Budget job to finish in <6h with 2× headroom.
bottlenecks.detection: Track agg.job_duration_seconds against a 4-week moving average — alert if current run >1.3× average or exceeds 12h absolute. Alert on agg.input_rows_per_sec dropping below 200K (indicates shuffle skew). Page if job end-time is within 2h of the worker kickoff deadline.

bottlenecks.title: Shuffle skew from Zipf-distributed hot queries
bottlenecks.trigger: Query frequency follows a power law — a handful of queries like 'facebook' (book's example: 930M hits) dominate volume. A group-by-query shuffle sends all rows for one query to a single reducer; with 50-concurrency sim budget, one hot reducer processes orders of magnitude more rows than peers, extending tail latency of the batch.
bottlenecks.symptom: Spark/MapReduce stage shows 49 of 50 tasks complete in minutes while 1–2 tasks run for hours; job duration dominated by stragglers; executor OOM on the hot-key reducer if it tries to hold all rows in memory; aggregated_weekly publish delayed even though most of the data is ready.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Apply salted group-by: hash queries into N=1000 sub-keys for the first aggregation pass, then a second pass merges sub-key partials. Alternatively enable Spark AQE (adaptive query execution) with skew-join handling, or pre-filter ultra-hot queries into a separate fast path using a CMS-based heavy-hitter detector at the mapper.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-task metrics: agg.task_duration_p99 / agg.task_duration_p50 ratio — alert if >5× (healthy jobs are ~2×). Track agg.task_input_bytes max vs median; alert on >10× skew. Monitor executor.peak_memory on straggler tasks to catch OOM risk early.

bottlenecks.title: Duplicate or out-of-order log ingestion corrupting frequency counts
bottlenecks.trigger: Analytics Logs upstream has sim failureRate 0.0002 and uses append-only Kafka with at-least-once semantics; API retries on log-emit failures can double-write rows. Over ~1.4B weekly rows, even a 0.1% duplication rate inflates frequency counts by ~1.4M row-events, biasing top-K rankings — especially for mid-frequency queries where ordering in top-5 is close.
bottlenecks.symptom: Autocomplete shows queries ranked higher than their true popularity (particularly noticeable for queries just above the top-5 cutoff); week-over-week frequency numbers jump inexplicably for queries tied to log-tier incidents; analyst ad-hoc queries on aggregated_weekly don't reconcile with raw-log spot-checks.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deduplicate during aggregation using (request_id, query, ts) as a unique key — API emits a UUID per log row, aggregator drops duplicates in a first-pass distinct. Alternatively, use Kafka exactly-once semantics with transactional producer. For ordering, window by event-time not processing-time and allow 1h watermark slack before closing a weekly window.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: agg.duplicate_rows_dropped_total / agg.input_rows_total — alert if ratio >0.5%. Reconciliation job: sample 100 queries/week and compare aggregated_weekly.frequency against an independent unsampled counter — alert on >5% discrepancy for any top-1000 query.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Aggregators are here For a search autocomplete system, the trie needs to know that "facebook" was searched 930M times and "facetious" was searched 8K times — otherwise it can't pick a top-5. That popularity signal starts as raw log rows in Analytics Logs, one per sampled keystroke: `('tree', 2019-10-01 22:01:01)`. But raw logs are useless to the Trie Build Worker — they're billions of rows with no ranking, no grouping, no frequency count. The Aggregator is the step that turns "a firehose of events" into "a clean table of (query, week, frequency)" that the worker can actually iterate over to build the trie. Without it, the worker would have to do a billion-row group-by every Sunday, and there'd be no intermediate table for analysts or debugging. ## What happens without it Skip the Aggregator and the Trie Build Worker has two bad choices: read raw logs directly (each weekly rebuild re-scans ~1.4B rows from scratch, job runtime balloons past the Sunday deadline) or give up on popularity-based ranking entirely. Users see a trie that's either stale (rebuild missed its window) or randomly ordered (no frequency data). Operators see the worker job timing out; analysts have no queryable table to answer "what's trending this week?" ## The number At 48K peak QPS with 1:10 sampling, Analytics Logs absorb **~4.8K rows/sec × 604,800 sec/week ≈ 2.9B rows/week**. The Aggregator collapses that down to **~10M distinct (query, week) rows** — a **290× reduction** before the worker ever touches the data. ## Trade-off You've accepted weekly staleness in exchange for a dead-simple batch pipeline instead of streaming aggregation.

aggdata.name: Aggregated Data
aggdata.summary: Aggregated weekly frequency table (query, time, frequency). Consumed by the trie build worker.

sections.heading: Role (book §Aggregated Data, Table 13-4)
sections.body: Book: '(query, time, frequency)' rows where 'time field represents the start time of a week' and 'frequency field is the sum of the occurrences for the corresponding query in that week.'

sections.heading: Why relational
sections.body: Only touched by batch jobs — no online QPS. SQL lets analysts run ad-hoc queries ('top growing queries this week') without building custom pipelines.

sections.heading: Size
sections.body: ~10M distinct queries × 52 weeks ≈ 520M rows/year. Trivial for modest Postgres or Hive.

gained: Scales to trillions of rows for free-form analysis

bottlenecks.title: Weekly worker full-table scan contends with analyst ad-hoc queries
bottlenecks.trigger: Trie Build Worker reads the entire current-week partition (~10M rows) in one pass during the Sunday rebuild. With sim concurrency cap of 200 and service times of 5–25ms per query, a worker doing a full SELECT while analysts run their own 'top growing queries this week' joins can saturate the connection pool and I/O bandwidth simultaneously.
bottlenecks.symptom: Worker job duration stretches from minutes to hours on Sunday rebuild; analyst queries time out or return after multi-minute waits; Postgres shows lock contention on aggregated_weekly; trie rebuild misses its weekly deadline, leaving Trie Cache serving stale top-K.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Partition aggregated_weekly by time (weekly partitions) so the worker only touches the current week's partition; add a read replica dedicated to the worker's bulk scan, leaving the primary for analyst/OLTP traffic; use COPY or server-side cursors with a 10K-row fetch size rather than loading all 10M rows into memory.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on aggdata.active_connections > 150 (75% of 200 cap) sustained 2min; track worker job duration against a 4-week moving average — alert if current run > 1.3× baseline; monitor pg_stat_activity for queries waiting on locks > 30s.

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded row growth from weekly snapshots accumulating across years
bottlenecks.trigger: Schema stores (query, week, frequency) with ~10M distinct queries/week × 52 weeks ≈ 520M rows/year, growing linearly. After 3–5 years, the table hits 1.5–2.5B rows. Indexes on (query, time) balloon to tens of GB, and the worker's weekly scan (even partitioned) slows as B-tree depth and autovacuum cost grow.
bottlenecks.symptom: Weekly worker job runtime trends upward month over month without a corresponding traffic increase; analyst queries that scan multi-week windows get progressively slower; autovacuum on aggregated_weekly starts running continuously, stealing I/O from foreground queries; disk usage alerts fire.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement a retention policy: drop partitions older than 2 years, or tier cold weeks to S3/Parquet via pg_partman + foreign tables; compress historical partitions with columnar extensions (Citus Columnar or BigQuery for archive); ensure only the most recent 4–8 weeks live in hot relational storage since the worker only needs the latest week for rebuilds.
bottlenecks.detection: Dashboard on aggdata.table_size_gb and aggdata.row_count with weekly growth rate — alert if growth exceeds 15% week-over-week or total size crosses 500GB; track worker scan time per partition and alert on > 2× historical median.

bottlenecks.title: Upsert write storm from aggregator publish overwhelming concurrency cap
bottlenecks.trigger: Aggregator writes ~10M rows/week to aggregated_weekly using `INSERT... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`. If the Spark/MapReduce job finishes its shuffle and flushes all partials at once, the write burst can briefly demand hundreds of concurrent connections against the sim's 200 concurrency budget, with 5–25ms per upsert implying ~50K upserts/sec needed to drain in 200s.
bottlenecks.symptom: Aggregator job's final write stage stalls or retries with 'too many connections' / deadlock errors; p99 write latency on aggregated_weekly spikes into hundreds of ms; analyst queries during the publish window block on row-level locks; publish timing slips, pushing trie rebuild window later on Sunday.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use batched multi-row INSERTs (1000 rows per statement) with a bounded writer pool (e.g., 20–50 parallel connections) rather than per-row upserts; stage writes to a temporary table and swap via `INSERT... SELECT` inside a transaction for atomic publish; alternatively use COPY into a staging table then MERGE to deduplicate — this bypasses the upsert hot path entirely.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: aggdata.writes_per_sec and aggdata.connection_wait_events during aggregator publish windows; alert if connection_wait > 0 or if the publish stage takes > 15min (normal should be 2–5min with batching); track deadlock_total counter — alert on any nonzero value.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Aggregated Data is here For a search autocomplete system that rebuilds its trie weekly, *something* has to hold the clean, ranked query-frequency table that the Trie Build Worker iterates over on Sunday. The Aggregators produce that table by rolling up billions of raw log rows into `(query, week, frequency)` tuples — but those results need to live in a queryable store so the worker can read them, and so analysts can answer questions like "what queries are trending this week?" without re-running the whole batch pipeline. That's what Aggregated Data is: the durable, queryable handoff point between the log-crunching pipeline and the trie-building pipeline. ## What happens without it Skip this table and the worker has to either re-aggregate raw logs from scratch every Sunday (doubling the batch runtime and risking missing the rebuild window) or consume the aggregator's output as a transient stream with no replay. If the worker crashes mid-build, there's nothing to restart from — you'd have to re-scan a week of raw logs. Analysts also lose their ability to eyeball ranking decisions; product teams get blind to what the autocomplete is actually learning. ## The number At ~10M distinct queries per week × 52 weeks = **520M rows/year**. Each row is tiny (query string + timestamp + bigint), so even a modest Postgres instance handles this comfortably — the worker's weekly scan touches only the current week's ~10M rows, not the full history. ## Trade-off You've accepted one more storage system to operate in exchange for decoupling the aggregation and trie-build stages, plus a free analytics surface.

worker.name: Trie Build Workers
worker.summary: Async servers that read aggregated data and build the trie data structure (with top-K cached at each node), then publish it to Trie DB and Trie Cache.

sections.heading: Role (book §Workers)
sections.body: Book: 'Workers are a set of servers that perform asynchronous jobs at regular intervals. They build the trie data structure and store it in Trie DB.'

sections.heading: Trie optimizations (book §Trie data structure)
sections.body:
Two optimizations the worker bakes in:
1. **Limit max prefix length** — book suggests p ≤ 50. Makes prefix lookup O(1).
2. **Cache top-k at each node** — book: 'we store top k most frequently used queries at each node.' So online lookup is: walk to node, return node.topK. Trade space for time.

sections.heading: Trie operations (book §Trie operations)
sections.body:
- **Create**: Worker builds from aggregated data.
- **Update option 1**: rebuild weekly, new trie replaces old. Book-recommended for scale.
- **Update option 2**: update individual node; ancestors must also update (they store top-k of descendants). Slow; only OK for small tries.
- **Delete**: handled by filter layer online + physical removal offline before next rebuild cycle.

sections.heading: Multiple tries (book §Wrap-up multi-language)
sections.body: For multi-language: 'we store Unicode characters in trie nodes.' For per-country: 'build different tries for different countries' and 'store tries in CDNs.'

lost: Book: 'we try to avoid this operation because it is slow' — all ancestors must update too

gained: Book's real-time follow-up path: 'change the ranking model and assign more weight to recent search queries'
lost: Harder state management than weekly batch

bottlenecks.title: Full-trie rebuild runtime outgrowing the weekly window
bottlenecks.trigger: Worker must ingest ~10M distinct (query, week, frequency) rows from aggregated_weekly and build a ~30M-node trie with top-5 cached at every node, then compute top-K via a recursive post-order pass that merges child heaps all the way to the root. With sim service times of 100–2000ms per task and concurrency cap of 50, the O(N log K) post-pass plus 6–9 GB of serialization write to Trie DB can exceed the Sunday rebuild window as data grows 0.4 GB/day.
bottlenecks.symptom: Weekly job duration trends upward month over month; Sunday rebuild slips into Monday, leaving Trie Cache serving last-week's snapshot beyond intended cadence; if job fails partway, no partial trie is publishable and the next cycle must start from scratch; on-call pages for 'trie-rebuild SLA breach' become routine.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Parallelize trie construction by first-letter (or shard-map bucket) so workers build independent sub-tries concurrently across the 50-concurrency budget; compute top-K bottom-up with a bounded heap (size K=5) per node rather than collecting all descendants; checkpoint intermediate sub-tries to object storage so a mid-job failure resumes rather than restarts; budget total runtime to <6h with 2× headroom and alert if forecast exceeds 12h.
bottlenecks.detection: Track worker.job_duration_seconds against a 4-week moving average — alert if current run >1.3× average or exceeds 12h absolute. Per-stage metrics: worker.ingest_seconds, worker.topk_compute_seconds, worker.publish_seconds — alert if any stage exceeds 2× its 4-week median. Page if job end-time is within 2h of cache-swap deadline.

bottlenecks.title: Atomic publish to Trie DB + Trie Cache risks torn or inconsistent trie versions
bottlenecks.trigger: Worker writes ~30M prefix rows (6–9 GB) to Trie DB then triggers Trie Cache to snapshot-load the new version. During the minutes-long write window, some shards see version W17 while others still on W16; if the worker crashes between DB publish and cache snapshot signal, cache and DB diverge — cache-miss fall-through reads from a newer DB than the cache expects, returning top-K for queries the cache doesn't yet know about.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cache-miss responses contain suggestions that disagree with cache-hit responses for sibling prefixes; users see jittery top-5 ordering across keystrokes; operators find cache.version and triedb.version mismatched post-incident; rollback is painful because old version rows may already have been overwritten in-place.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Write each new trie to a versioned namespace (triedb.v=trie-2026-W17) rather than mutating current rows, and flip a single pointer (current_version) atomically after all shards confirm write completion; use two-phase publish — (1) worker writes all shards + verifies row counts, (2) worker signals cache to load-and-swap, (3) worker updates pointer only after cache ACKs. Keep N=2 prior versions resident for instant rollback.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: worker.publish_version_skew (count of distinct versions across Trie DB shards during publish) — alert if >1 for >60s outside publish window. Post-publish consistency probe: sample 1000 random prefixes, compare cache vs DB top-K — alert on any mismatch. Track worker.publish_phase gauge; alert if stuck in phase 1 or 2 for >30min.

bottlenecks.title: Memory pressure during in-process trie construction for 30M nodes
bottlenecks.trigger: Worker builds the entire trie in-memory before serializing: ~30M nodes × ~200–300B/node (children map + top-K entries + word/freq metadata) ≈ 6–9 GB of heap per trie generation. The recursive top-K post-pass also allocates transient heaps at every internal node. Multi-language extension (Unicode nodes) or per-country tries multiplies this further — a naive JVM/Python worker can OOM on a single commodity box.
bottlenecks.symptom: Worker process OOM-kills partway through construction, losing hours of work and forcing a restart from scratch; GC pauses stretch 100ms+ service times into multi-second stalls, blowing the sim's upper bound; horizontal scaling is impossible because the design assumes one worker sees the whole trie.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Build sub-tries per shard-map bucket in separate worker processes (each holds ~1/8th the nodes, ~1 GB heap) and merge only top-level roots at publish; use compressed radix/DAWG representation to collapse shared suffixes (typical 3–5× node reduction); intern query strings across top-K entries since hot queries like 'facebook' repeat in many ancestors' top-K; size worker hosts at ≥3× measured peak heap to absorb GC headroom.
bottlenecks.detection: Metrics: worker.heap_used_bytes peak per stage, worker.gc_pause_p99_ms, worker.oom_kills_total. Alert on heap_used >70% of container limit at any stage, gc_pause_p99 >500ms, or any oom_kill event. Capacity-plan quarterly by projecting aggregated_weekly row-count growth (0.4 GB/day) against worker RAM budget.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Trie Build Workers are here For a search autocomplete system that promises top-5 suggestions in under 100ms, the serving path *cannot* afford to compute rankings at request time. The whole trick is that when a user types "tr", the Trie Cache already has `[("true", 35), ("try", 29), ("tree", 10)]` precomputed and waiting. But *something* has to do that precomputation — walk through ~10M distinct queries from the Aggregated Data table, insert each into a trie, and then run a post-order pass that bubbles up the top-5 to every one of ~30M trie nodes. That's the Trie Build Workers' job: they absorb hours of CPU and memory work offline so that the online read path is just a pointer walk. ## What happens without them Skip the worker and you have two bad options. Either the API computes top-K on every keystroke (scanning frequency data live — blows the 100ms budget immediately, Trie DB melts at 48K QPS), or the Trie Cache and Trie DB sit empty because nothing ever populates them. Users see a blank dropdown; operators see a perfectly healthy aggregation pipeline feeding nowhere; the filter layer has nothing to filter. ## The number The worker processes **~10M distinct queries/week** from aggregated_weekly and produces a trie with top-5 at every node — roughly **30M nodes × ~250 bytes ≈ 7.5 GB** of precomputed answers. That one weekly job replaces **~29 billion online ranking computations** (48K QPS × 604,800 sec/week), each of which would otherwise have to finish in under 100ms. ## Trade-off Freshness lags by up to a week — the price paid for making the read path trivially fast.

operations.title: Trie rebuild cycle (weekly)
operations.name: Trie rebuild cycle (weekly)
operations.description: Book §Data gathering service (Figure 13-9). Analytics Logs → Aggregators → Aggregated Data → Workers build trie → publish to Trie DB + Trie Cache.

steps.title: Aggregators read a week of analytics logs
steps.action: Book §Analytics Logs: append-only, unindexed. Each row is (query, time). Sampled writes: 1 of every N real requests.

steps.title: Aggregator rolls logs into (query, week, frequency)
steps.action: Book §Aggregators: 'we need to aggregate data so it can be easily processed.' Book's assumption: 'trie is rebuilt weekly,' so group by week.

steps.title: Persist aggregated weekly table
steps.action: Book §Aggregated Data: (query, time, frequency) rows. Analysts can also run ad-hoc queries against this table.
steps.codeOrCommand:
INSERT INTO aggregated_weekly (query, time, frequency) VALUES (?,?,?)
ON CONFLICT (query, time) DO UPDATE SET frequency = EXCLUDED.frequency

steps.title: Workers build trie with top-K cached at every node
steps.action: Book §Workers. Two optimizations baked in: (1) limit max prefix length to ~50, making lookup O(1); (2) 'store top k most frequently used queries at each node.'
steps.codeOrCommand:
trie = Trie
for (query, freq) in aggregated_weekly.all: trie.insert(query, freq) # Post-pass: compute top-K at every node
def compute_topk(node): all_items = for child in node.children.values: compute_topk(child) all_items.extend(child.topK) if node.is_word: all_items.append((node.word, node.freq)) node.topK = heapq.nlargest(5, all_items, key=lambda x: x[1])
compute_topk(trie.root)

steps.title: Worker serializes trie into Trie DB
steps.action: Book §Trie DB option 1 (doc store) or 2 (hash-table form). Either way, the worker writes the full new trie so the cache can replenish from it.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Option 2 — hash-table form (book)
for prefix, node in trie.walk: triedb.put(prefix, {"children": list(node.children), "topK": node.topK})

steps.title: Worker snapshots Trie Cache with new version
steps.action: Book: 'Trie Cache … takes a weekly snapshot of the DB.' Cache is atomically swapped to the new version; old generation freed after in-flight reads drain.

steps.title: Subsequent suggest requests have the term stripped
steps.action: Filter layer removes the term from any top-K it sees. User-visible takedown is sub-minute.

steps.title: Offline job removes term from aggregated data
steps.action: Book: 'Unwanted suggestions are removed physically from the database asynchronically so the correct data set will be used to build trie in the next update cycle.'

steps.title: Next weekly rebuild excludes the term from the trie

tradeoffs.chosen: Trie with top-K cached at every node
tradeoffs.rationale: Answers any prefix in O(P) with zero sorting on the hot path. Costs extra memory and makes inserts more expensive, but inserts happen offline and serving is what the user feels.

tradeoffs.chosen: Daily (or weekly) batch rebuild from logs
tradeoffs.rationale: Simple, testable, and cheap. Accepts that trending queries lag by one rebuild cycle; a streaming pipeline is the follow-up when that lag becomes a product problem.

tradeoffs.chosen: Range-shard by first characters of the prefix
tradeoffs.rationale: Locality-friendly and easy to reason about, but popular first letters (e.g. "a", "s") go hot. A shard-map manager reshards on observed load rather than using a fixed split.

Most users retype the same prefixes within an hour, so a short browser cache eliminates a big fraction of requests. Downside: newly trending queries remain invisible to a given user for up to an hour.

tradeoffs.chosen: Post-rank filter layer rather than pre-index blocklist
tradeoffs.rationale: Keeps the trie neutral and lets policy evolve without a full rebuild, at the cost of a small per-request filtering step.
